Conditional

/kun-DISH-uh-nul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Conditional means dependent on something else being true or happening first.

Conditional means dependent on something else being true or happening first. The job offer was conditional on passing a background check, so nothing was final until the results came in.

Worked Example

A college accepted Maya for the fall semester, but the acceptance was conditional: she had to earn at least a B in her final semester of calculus. The admissions letter spelled it out plainly. If the grade came in lower, the offer would be withdrawn. Maya taped the letter above her desk and studied harder than she ever had, because her place in the class depended on meeting that one requirement first.

The acceptance depended on another thing being true first (the calculus grade), which is exactly what conditional means.

How Conditional Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

dependent

dependent: relying on something else to happen or hold true

provisional

provisional: in effect only for now, until conditions are settled

Antonyms

unconditional

unconditional: given with no requirements attached

absolute

absolute: complete and not limited by any condition

How Strong Is It? — qualified → contingent → conditional

qualified vs. conditional

qualified vs. conditional: A qualified approval merely adds a few reservations, while a conditional approval does not take effect at all unless its requirement is met.

contingent vs. conditional

contingent vs. conditional: A conditional offer names a specific requirement that must be satisfied, and a contingent deal goes further, hanging entirely on an uncertain outside event that neither side controls.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: together, with

Root — dit

Root — dit: from Latin dicere, to say, by way of condicio, terms spoken and agreed together

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: the act or state of

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: relating to

Put it together

Put it together: Conditional traces back to Latin condicio, 'an agreement, the terms spoken together,' built on con- (together) plus dicere (to say). A conditional offer literally comes with spoken terms attached: something must be stated and satisfied before the deal stands.

Use the root in a new word: verdict

Use the root in a new word: verdict: The jury delivered its verdict, literally a 'truly said' decision from the Latin roots verus and dicere, and the courtroom fell silent.
